views.name: order_items_enriched
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  oi.order_id,
  oi.order_item_id,
  oi.product_id,
  oi.seller_id,
  oi.shipping_limit_date,
  oi.price,
  oi.freight_value,
  o.customer_id,
  o.order_status,
  o.order_purchase_timestamp,
  c.customer_unique_id,
  c.customer_zip_code_prefix,
  c.customer_city,
  c.customer_state,
  s.seller_zip_code_prefix,
  s.seller_city,
  s.seller_state,
  p.product_category_name,
  t.product_category_name_english
FROM order_items AS oi
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
LEFT JOIN customers AS c
  ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT JOIN sellers AS s
  ON oi.seller_id = s.seller_id
LEFT JOIN products AS p
  ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
LEFT JOIN product_category_name_translation AS t
  ON p.product_category_name = t.product_category_name

params.when_to_use: List or inspect order items with related order, customer, seller and product attributes at the item-level grain (one row per order_item_id within an order). | Join item-level price/freight to order and customer attributes for analyses that need per-item monetary fields without aggregating (e.g., compute per-item margin, item-level shipping delay, or item-level features for modeling). | Filter or cohort by order-level attributes while preserving item-level detail (e.g., all items for orders placed in a date range or by order_status), because the view keeps the one-row-per-order_item_id grain. | Build features that require both product category and translated category name alongside item price/seller and customer location at the item level.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view when you need order-level aggregates (e.g., total order revenue, number of items per order) — using it directly and aggregating without deduplicating order-level fields can double-count or mis-count values because order attributes are repeated for each item. | Avoid using it for customer-level analytics (e.g., lifetime value, number of orders per customer) without first aggregating to customer grain; the view returns one row per order_item_id so naive counts will overcount items as customers. | Do not use it to compute payment-level metrics or reconcile payments to orders — payments are a separate entity (see order_payments_aggregated) and this view has no payment fields, so joining naively may produce multiplicative rows if payments are many-to-one with orders. | Avoid using it as a canonical source of the latest order status when order status changes over time; this view pulls order_status from orders but does not handle historical or ranked status — it may return a single status per order but not necessarily the latest event if multiple status records exist elsewhere. | Do not use this view when you need normalized product or dimensional keys (e.g., a canonical product dimension) — product attributes are present but not normalized or deduplicated for dimension lookups.
params.comparison: use order_payments_aggregated instead when you need order-level payment aggregates — order_payments_aggregated is an AGG targeted at payments and prevents row-multiplication between items and payments. | use customer_order_agg instead when you need customer-level summaries (orders per customer, customer lifetime spend) — customer_order_agg is aggregated to customer grain and avoids counting each order_item as a separate customer-level event. | use product_category_sales instead when you need pre-aggregated sales by product category — product_category_sales provides aggregated metrics by category, whereas order_items_enriched is item-level and would require aggregation. | use seller_location_lookup instead when you only need seller location attributes — seller_location_lookup is a JOIN focused on sellers and may be de-duplicated at the seller grain, while order_items_enriched repeats seller attributes per order item. | use orders_with_review instead when your analysis revolves around order-level review metadata — orders_with_review focuses on orders and reviews, and will be at the order grain (or include review-specific logic) unlike this item-level view. | use orders_latest_status_rank when you require the latest or ranked order status over time — that view handles ranking/timeliness of status, while order_items_enriched surfaces the order_status as stored on orders without ranking.

views.description: One row per order_items line enriched with order header, customer and seller attributes plus product category translation. Useful for revenue, fulfillment, product- and geography-level analyses where line-item-level measures are needed. | Use for: calculate order-line revenue, average price or freight by product category or geography; join reviews/payments to line items for per-line profitability; analyze seller performance by delivered orders and revenue

views.name: order_payments_aggregated
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id,
  COUNT(*) AS payment_count,
  SUM(payment_value) AS payment_value_total,
  MIN(payment_value) AS payment_value_min,
  MAX(payment_value) AS payment_value_max
FROM order_payments
GROUP BY order_id

params.when_to_use: Calculate per-order payment-level summaries (for each order_id): number of payment records, total paid value, minimum single-payment value, maximum single-payment value. | Join these per-order payment aggregates back to order-level data when you need payment counts or payment totals at the order grain (one row per order). | Detect orders with multiple payments or no payments (after an outer join) by using payment_count = 0 or >1 at the order_id level. | Compute order-level metrics that treat each payment record equally (COUNT(*) counts payment rows, SUM aggregates payment_value as stored).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need payment-level detail (e.g., individual payment method, payment timestamp, payment_id) — this view collapses all payments to the order grain and discards row-level identifiers; you will lose the ability to filter or group by payment attributes. | Do not use when you need a different grain than order_id (e.g., customer-level, product-level, seller-level, daily totals). Reusing it for customer or product metrics will silently produce incorrect results because it aggregates payments per order and not per customer/product. | Do not use when you need cohort or filtered counts of payments defined by attributes on the payment rows (for example, counting only successful payments, or payments within a date range) because the view does not apply any payment_row filters — you will miscount or include unintended payment rows. | Do not use for percentiles, medians, or other non-min/max distribution summaries — this view only provides SUM, MIN, MAX, and COUNT, so reusing it for those statistics will be incomplete or wrong. | Do not use when you need distinct counts of payment sources or unique payment_ids per order; COUNT(*) is a raw row count and may double-count logical payments if duplicates exist. | Do not use if your downstream aggregation will aggregate again over payment rows expecting independent payment-level observations (for example, averaging payment_value across orders by summing payment_value_total and dividing by order count is fine, but averaging payment_value across payments requires using raw payment rows). Re-aggregating can produce biased results if the intention was to weight by payment rows differently.
params.comparison: use customer_order_agg instead when you need customer-level aggregates (same DB, different grain) — customer_order_agg aggregates at the customer (or customer-order) level and is appropriate when the analysis question is per-customer, whereas order_payments_aggregated is strictly per-order. | use order_items_enriched when your metric should be driven by items or products on the order (same DB, different dimension) — order_items_enriched preserves item/product attributes and item-level quantities/prices that are lost when using order-level payment aggregates. | use orders_latest_status_rank when you need the latest order lifecycle status or time-ranked order records — orders_latest_status_rank provides rank/time context per order which payment aggregates do not contain. | use seller_location_lookup when you need seller geolocation or seller attributes joined in — order_payments_aggregated contains no seller fields and cannot substitute for a lookup join when filtering by seller location. | use leads_closed_enriched or other JOIN views when your analysis depends on enriched order metadata (lead/source/customer enrichment) — those JOINs preserve contextual attributes that are not present in this payment-only aggregation.

views.description: One row per order with aggregated payment metrics: total payment_value, count of payment rows, and breakdown metrics helpful to reconcile payments to order totals or to examine payment method usage. Use when comparing order-level amounts or joining to orders/order_items. | Use for: compare aggregated payments to order line totals to find mismatches; identify orders with multiple payment attempts or split payments; compute revenue per order after aggregating payment rows

views.name: orders_with_review
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  o.customer_id,
  o.order_status,
  o.order_purchase_timestamp,
  o.order_approved_at,
  o.order_delivered_carrier_date,
  o.order_delivered_customer_date,
  o.order_estimated_delivery_date,
  r.review_id,
  r.review_score,
  r.review_creation_date
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN order_reviews AS r
  ON o.order_id = r.order_id

params.when_to_use: When you need one row per order with any associated single review fields included (i.e., inspect order-level fields together with review columns that are NULL when no review exists). | When you want to list orders and also show review metadata for auditing or display purposes, accepting that orders with multiple reviews will appear multiple times (one row per matching review). | When performing joins that require review identifiers or scores at the order-level (for example, showing order details alongside the review_id and review_score for each matching review). | When you want to filter or sort primarily by order attributes (order_purchase_timestamp, order_status, etc.) and optionally reference review columns directly.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to produce aggregates per order (e.g., average score per order, count of reviews per order, total review_count): because this view preserves one row per order-review match, aggregating without deduplication will mis-count duplicates or produce incorrect aggregates when orders have multiple reviews. | Do not use this view as the canonical one-row-per-order source when orders may have multiple reviews and you expect exactly one row per order: the LEFT JOIN will create multiple rows for orders that have more than one matching review_id, producing an incorrect grain. | Do not use this view to compute customer-level metrics (e.g., customer lifetime review average, number of reviewed orders per customer) without first aggregating to the customer grain: using the view directly risks double-counting orders that have multiple reviews. | Do not use this view to filter cohorts by 'has review' versus 'no review' by simply testing for NULL review_id in downstream joins that then aggregate, unless you explicitly deduplicate reviews per order: the presence of multiple review rows will distort cohort sizes and rates. | Do not use this view when you need the most recent review per order only (e.g., latest review_score per order): this view does not apply any ranking or filtering to pick a single review; it returns all linked reviews. | Do not use this view when you need true order-only datasets for joins that expect unique order_id: because order_id may appear multiple times, downstream joins assuming uniqueness can produce row explosion or wrong multiplicative joins.
params.comparison: use order_payments_aggregated instead when you need order-level aggregated payment metrics (same order grain) — it provides pre-aggregated numeric payment measures while orders_with_review includes raw review rows and can multiply when joined with payment aggregates if not deduplicated. | use customer_order_agg instead when you need customer-level aggregates (e.g., counts, averages across a customer's orders) — customer_order_agg already rolls up to customer grain, avoiding double-counting caused by multiple review rows in orders_with_review. | use orders_latest_status_rank instead when you need one canonical row per order with the latest status (same order grain) — orders_latest_status_rank enforces uniqueness and status ranking, whereas orders_with_review may return multiple rows per order due to reviews. | use order_items_enriched when your question concerns order composition (items, product-level details) — order_items_enriched has item-level granularity and enriched product data; joining it directly to orders_with_review risks multiplying rows further unless you first choose a single review per order. | use seller_location_lookup or product_dimensions_normalized for reference lookups (joins that add static attributes) — those sibling joins are safe for enrichment because they preserve uniqueness for their respective keys; orders_with_review is a join that may introduce multiplicity because of the 1-to-many relationship from orders to order_reviews. | use leads_closed_enriched only for lead-related analyses — it has a different business domain and aggregation; do not substitute orders_with_review when you need closed-lead-level details.

views.description: One row per order enriched with review information when present (left join). Useful to analyze how review_score relates to order attributes, delivery timing, or customer segments. | Use for: correlate delivery delays with low review_score; compute average review_score by customer or product (join needed from order_items_enriched); identify orders missing reviews

views.name: customer_order_agg
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  o.customer_id,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders,
  COUNT(oi.order_item_id) AS total_items,
  SUM(oi.price + COALESCE(oi.freight_value,0)) AS total_revenue,
  CASE WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) = 0 THEN 0 ELSE SUM(oi.price + COALESCE(oi.freight_value,0)) / COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) END AS average_order_value
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi
  ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
GROUP BY o.customer_id

params.when_to_use: Calculate per-customer aggregates about orders and items over the set of orders present in the orders table (e.g., "For each customer, how many orders did they place, how many order items in total, total revenue across those items, and the average order value?"). | Build customer-level features that summarize order counts, item counts, and item-based revenue using order_items rows joined to orders (e.g., customer lifetime value approximations that are based on summing order_items.price + freight). | Reporting where the desired row-level grain is one row per customer and NULL/no-orders customers should still appear (LEFT JOIN preserves customers with zero items; average_order_value returns 0 when order count is 0).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not reuse when you need order-level metrics (wrong grain). This view is aggregated to customer_id; using it for order-level joins or to answer "what happened on order X" will silently produce over-aggregated/duplicated results. | Do not reuse for item-level analyses that require the raw order_items rows (wrong grain and lost detail). total_items is a pre-aggregated count; you cannot recover per-item attributes or distinct item counts by product from this view. | Do not reuse when you need revenue measures that should include columns not present here (e.g., discounts, taxes, adjustments, or payment-specific amounts). The view sums only oi.price + COALESCE(oi.freight_value,0), so any missing components in order_items or other tables will be omitted, causing undercounted revenue. | Do not reuse when you require distinct-item counting semantics different from COUNT(oi.order_item_id). The view uses COUNT(oi.order_item_id) which counts rows; if you need DISTINCT product_id per customer or unique SKUs, this will be incorrect. | Do not reuse for cohorts or filters applied at the order_item level after aggregation (filtering/segmenting by item attributes). Because aggregation happens across joined rows, applying item-level filters later to this aggregated result will be impossible or incorrect. | Do not reuse when orders can have multiple order_items and you want to count distinct orders weighted by items differently. The view uses COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) for total_orders and sums items/revenue across items — reusing it to compute e.g., average price per item vs per order may misrepresent the intended metric. | Do not reuse when you need precise handling of customers with zero orders vs customers absent from orders table. This view groups by o.customer_id from orders; customers not present in orders will not appear. It preserves customers who appear in orders but have no order_items (due to LEFT JOIN), but customers with no orders at all are excluded.
params.comparison: use order_items_enriched instead when you need row-level item detail or additional item attributes (it is a JOIN-level view that preserves item granularity) — customer_order_agg is aggregated to customer_id and loses per-item columns. | use order_payments_aggregated instead when you need payment-based revenue/amounts or payment-level aggregations (it is an AGG focused on payments) — customer_order_agg sums order_items.price + freight only and ignores payment adjustments/refunds. | use orders_with_review instead when you need order-level review/feedback context or to filter orders by review status (it is a JOIN view that preserves orders and review info) — customer_order_agg aggregates away order-level review details. | use orders_latest_status_rank when you need the latest status per order or to filter orders by their most recent status (it is a RANK view at order grain) — customer_order_agg aggregates across all orders and cannot be used to pick orders by latest status. | use product_category_sales when you need sales aggregated by product category (it is an AGG at product/category grain) — customer_order_agg is aggregated by customer and cannot substitute for category-level metrics.

views.description: One row per customer_id with aggregated order and spend metrics: total_orders, total_items (count of order_items), total_revenue (sum of price+freight), average_order_value. Useful for RFM, customer lifetime value estimation and segmentation. | Use for: compute customer lifetime revenue and average order value; segment customers by spend or order frequency; join to customer attributes or geolocation for regional analysis

views.name: product_category_sales
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  p.product_category_name,
  t.product_category_name_english,
  COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders_count,
  COUNT(oi.order_item_id) AS items_sold,
  SUM(oi.price + COALESCE(oi.freight_value,0)) AS revenue
FROM order_items AS oi
LEFT JOIN products AS p
  ON oi.product_id = p.product_id
LEFT JOIN product_category_name_translation AS t
  ON p.product_category_name = t.product_category_name
GROUP BY p.product_category_name, t.product_category_name_english

params.when_to_use: Get sales metrics aggregated at the product category name level (one row per product_category_name) — e.g., “for each product category, how many orders included at least one item, how many item rows were sold, and total revenue (price + freight)?” | Produce a report that needs the product_category_name_english label alongside the original category name when a 1:1 translation exists in product_category_name_translation. | Compare relative sizes of categories by orders_count, items_sold, or revenue where duplicates of product_category_name should be combined.
params.when_not_to_use: If you need metrics at the order level (one row per order) — this view counts DISTINCT order_id per category, so reusing it as if it were an orders table will under/over-count when orders contain items from multiple categories. | If you need to filter by order attributes (date, customer, status) before aggregating — this view aggregates across all order_items before filters; applying filters to the aggregated results can produce incorrect cohorts. Filters on order-level or item-level columns must be applied before grouping (use a join/source that preserves row-level order/order_item rows). | If you need to attribute revenue differently (e.g., exclude freight, include discounts, use payment records) — revenue here is SUM(price + COALESCE(freight_value, 0)) from order_items only and does not account for payments, refunds, discounts stored elsewhere, or distributed revenue allocations; reusing it for net revenue or payment-based metrics will be wrong. | If you need counts of unique customers, unique sellers, or distinct SKUs per category — this view only provides DISTINCT order_id and count of order_item_id, so it will mislead if you assume other distinct counts. | If you require complete translation coverage — product_category_name_english is joined with a LEFT JOIN to a translation table; missing translations will result in NULLs. Do not reuse assuming every category has an English label. | If you need the underlying item-level detail (e.g., to break down by product_id, order_item_id or to apply item-level filters) — this view is aggregated and loses item-level granularity.
params.comparison: use order_items_enriched (JOIN) instead when you need item-level rows with product attributes or want to apply filters at the order_item level before aggregating — it preserves the original grain so you can compute custom aggregates safely. | use order_payments_aggregated (AGG) instead when you need payment-based revenue figures or to match revenue to payments/refunds — it aggregates at the payment/order level and will reflect actual paid amounts rather than item price+freight. | use customer_order_agg (AGG) instead when you need metrics rolled up by customer (cohort by customer) rather than by product category — it has the customer grain which this view does not provide. | use orders_with_review (JOIN) or orders_latest_status_rank (RANK) when you need order-level attributes or status/review information joined into aggregates — those sibling views keep order-context necessary for cohorting by order status or review presence. | use product_dimensions_normalized (NORM) when you need authoritative product/category keys or normalized product attributes — it provides cleaned/normalized product/category fields that may avoid NULLs/mismatches present here due to direct joins.

views.description: Sales aggregated by product_category_name (category from products) with counts and revenue. Keeps category translation for English label. Useful for category-level performance and trend analysis when joined to time buckets. | Use for: rank categories by revenue or items sold; track category mix over time (join to orders.order_purchase_timestamp); compare category performance across seller regions

views.name: seller_location_lookup
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  s.seller_id,
  s.seller_zip_code_prefix,
  s.seller_city,
  s.seller_state,
  g.geolocation_lat,
  g.geolocation_lng,
  g.geolocation_city,
  g.geolocation_state
FROM sellers AS s
LEFT JOIN geolocation AS g
  ON s.seller_zip_code_prefix = g.geolocation_zip_code_prefix

params.when_to_use: Look up seller-level static attributes (seller_zip_code_prefix, seller_city, seller_state) and the geolocation row(s) that match that seller_zip_code_prefix — use when you need to enrich seller rows with one (or multiple) geolocation rows keyed by zip code. | Enrich a dataset at the exact grain of a seller (one row per seller) with latitude/longitude and geolocation city/state — when downstream joins will remain at seller_id granularity. | Spatial or location-based joins where precision at the seller_zip_code_prefix level is acceptable (e.g., mapping sellers to approximate coordinates or grouping sellers by geolocation_city/state).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when you need one unique geolocation per seller and the geolocation table contains multiple rows per zip_code_prefix — this LEFT JOIN can multiply seller rows and silently over-count metrics. | Do not use when the desired grain is geolocation (one row per lat/lng) rather than seller — the view is keyed by seller_id; flipping the grain will produce duplicates or drop geolocation rows without sellers. | Do not use when you need historical or time-scoped seller locations — this view uses current sellers and geolocation join only on zip prefix; it does not capture time/versioned addresses. | Do not use for aggregations that count distinct entities without additional de-duplication logic — because multiple geolocation matches per zip_prefix will inflate counts, sums, and averages if aggregated directly. | Do not use when you need exact point-level matching between seller addresses and geolocation rows by full postal code or address — the join is only on seller_zip_code_prefix and can be imprecise.
params.comparison: use order_items_enriched instead when you need seller attributes joined at the order-item grain — order_items_enriched already contains seller-related enrichment at the order line level, avoiding manual re-join and potential row multiplication. | use leads_closed_enriched instead when you need seller-like enrichment for lead entities — leads_closed_enriched is tailored to leads and may include de-duplication/filters appropriate for that cohort, whereas seller_location_lookup is seller-centric. | use product_dimensions_normalized when the downstream needs normalized, de-duplicated dimension records rather than a direct LEFT JOIN on a prefix — product_dimensions_normalized provides a normalized dimension shape suitable for safe joins at multiple grains. | use an aggregated geolocation mapping (not present among siblings) or construct a deduplicated geolocation lookup when you require exactly one lat/lng per zip_code_prefix — unlike this view, an aggregated lookup would avoid silent row multiplication.

views.description: One row per seller_id enriched with geolocation (lat/lng) by matching seller_zip_code_prefix to geolocation rows. Because geolocation may have multiple rows per prefix, this preserves all matching lat/lng points to support spatial aggregations or centroid calculations downstream. | Use for: map seller densities or compute shipping distances; aggregate seller performance by geographic clusters; compute nearest-seller analyses (requires further spatial logic)

views.name: orders_latest_status_rank
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id,
  customer_id,
  order_status,
  order_purchase_timestamp,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_purchase_timestamp DESC) AS purchase_rank
FROM orders

params.when_to_use: Find the most recent orders per customer or rank a customer's orders by purchase time (e.g., “show each customer's orders with a purchase_rank where 1 = most recent”). | Filter to a particular purchase_rank (for example, select only purchase_rank = 1 to get each customer's latest order) while preserving order-level columns and original order timestamps. | Analyses that need order-level detail (order_id, customer_id, order_status, order_purchase_timestamp) annotated with the customer's relative recency of that order.
params.when_not_to_use: Any aggregation across orders expecting aggregated metrics per customer (e.g., total_spend_per_customer) — WHY: this view is at the order grain (one row per order) and only provides a window rank; it does not sum/aggregate payment or item amounts, so aggregating without joining proper payment/item aggregates can undercount or double-count. | Questions that need the most recent order per customer but also require aggregated payment or item-level details (e.g., total_value_of_latest_order) — WHY: this view does not contain payment or item totals; joining directly to order_items or payments may be necessary and must be done after selecting the desired purchase_rank to avoid inflating totals. | Filtering by cohort definitions other than customer-based recency (e.g., cohort by product category or seller location) — WHY: the RANK is computed partitioned only by customer_id and ordered by order_purchase_timestamp; using it for non-customer partitions yields incorrect cohorts. | Using purchase_rank as a stable unique identifier for deduplication across different partitioning logic — WHY: RANK() can produce ties (same timestamp -> same rank) and there can be multiple rows with the same purchase_rank per customer; it does not guarantee a single row per rank unless breaking ties is handled. | Assuming purchase_rank reflects chronological order across all customers (global recency) — WHY: the window PARTITION BY customer_id makes rank relative per customer, not a global order-time ranking. | Joining this view into aggregations that expect one row per customer without first filtering to a single rank (e.g., joining into a customer-level table without restricting to purchase_rank = 1) — WHY: joining order-level rows will multiply customer-level rows and produce inflated counts or sums.
params.comparison: use customer_order_agg instead when you need customer-level aggregated metrics (same entity: customer) — it has aggregated metrics per customer whereas orders_latest_status_rank is order-grain with window ranks. | use order_payments_aggregated instead when you need payment totals per order (same entity: order_id) — it provides aggregated payment amounts per order; orders_latest_status_rank only provides order-level metadata and rank, not payment sums. | use order_items_enriched instead when you need item-level or product-level enrichment joined to orders (same starting table: orders) — order_items_enriched contains item/product joins and quantities/prices; orders_latest_status_rank lacks item/payment detail and should not be used to compute revenue or item counts. | use orders_with_review instead when you need review presence or review text associated with orders (same entity: order_id) — orders_with_review includes review join info; orders_latest_status_rank does not indicate whether an order has a review and could mislead if used to infer review-related cohorts. | use leads_closed_enriched when analyzing lead/sales funnel contexts joined to seller/product or lead metadata (different focus) — leads_closed_enriched contains lead-specific enrichment; orders_latest_status_rank is focused on order recency per customer and lacks lead fields. | use product_category_sales or product_dimensions_normalized when analyzing product- or category-level aggregates (different grain: product/category) — those views aggregate or normalize product attributes, whereas orders_latest_status_rank is order-grain and only suitable for customer-order recency questions. | use seller_location_lookup when you need seller geolocation or normalized seller metadata for geographic analyses — seller_location_lookup contains seller metadata; orders_latest_status_rank does not carry seller location and should not be used alone for geographic rollups.

views.description: One row per order_id with rank ordering by order_purchase_timestamp (most recent = 1). Useful as a building block for selecting latest orders or recent-order cohorts; exposes purchase_rank so downstream filters can implement top-K or recent-window logic. | Use for: find each customer's most recent order(s); build recency cohorts or compute time-to-repeat metrics; filter to top-N recent orders per customer by WHERE purchase_rank <= N

views.name: product_dimensions_normalized
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  product_id,
  product_category_name,
  CAST(product_name_lenght AS REAL) AS product_name_lenght,
  CAST(product_description_lenght AS REAL) AS product_description_lenght,
  CAST(product_photos_qty AS REAL) AS product_photos_qty,
  CAST(product_weight_g AS REAL) AS product_weight_g,
  CAST(product_length_cm AS REAL) AS product_length_cm,
  CAST(product_height_cm AS REAL) AS product_height_cm,
  CAST(product_width_cm AS REAL) AS product_width_cm,
  CASE
    WHEN product_length_cm IS NULL OR product_height_cm IS NULL OR product_width_cm IS NULL THEN NULL
    ELSE COALESCE(product_length_cm,0) * COALESCE(product_height_cm,0) * COALESCE(product_width_cm,0)
  END AS volume_cm3
FROM products

params.when_to_use: Get descriptive attributes for a single product_id or to look up product-level static attributes (category name, name/description lengths, photo count, weight, dimensions, computed volume). | Join product-level attributes into analyses whose grain is one row per product (e.g., product profiling, product quality dashboards, feature tables keyed by product_id). | Perform aggregations that legitimately reduce product rows to summary statistics (e.g., AVG(product_weight_g) across products, distribution of volume_cm3) — provided aggregation is explicit and you understand input is one row per product.
params.when_not_to_use: As a source for order- or order_item-level measures (e.g., to compute revenue per product in orders) — WHY: this view is at product grain (one row per product). Joining it into an order_items-level query without careful multiplicity control can silently duplicate product attributes across multiple order lines, producing inflated aggregations. | As a cohort or time-filtered product list (e.g., 'products sold in June' or 'products active last quarter') — WHY: the view selects from the base products table only and contains no sales/time filters. Reusing it will return all products, not cohort-limited sets. | When you need seller- or marketplace-scoped product attributes (e.g., per seller inventory or per marketplace listing) — WHY: there is no seller_id or seller-scoped key; using it assumes product attributes are global, which may be incorrect if products vary by seller. | When you need robust null-handling or unit-normalization beyond basic casts — WHY: numeric columns are cast to REAL but original NULLs are preserved (volume_cm3 returns NULL if any dimension is NULL). This may lead to unexpected NULLs in downstream numeric calculations if not handled explicitly. | For row-count based metrics (e.g., number of distinct products sold in an order) without de-duplication — WHY: reusing the view without DISTINCT or proper joins can miscount because it represents product catalog rows, not sold instances.
params.comparison: use order_items_enriched instead when you need product attributes combined with order-item context — it has order_item grain and includes multiplicity keys (order_id, item_id) so aggregations to sales are correct; product_dimensions_normalized only has product-level attributes. | use product_category_sales instead when you need aggregated sales metrics per category — it has pre-aggregated sales measures by category, whereas product_dimensions_normalized only provides category name and raw product attributes. | use customer_order_agg or order_payments_aggregated when your analysis is customer- or order-level with monetary aggregates — those sibling views provide order/payment aggregates and proper grains; product_dimensions_normalized lacks order/payment context and will not correctly represent monetary metrics. | use seller_location_lookup when you need seller or location context for products — seller_location_lookup provides seller/location keys; product_dimensions_normalized has no seller/location identifiers and cannot be used for seller-scoped joins.

views.description: One row per product_id projecting product physical attributes with NULL-preserving casts and derived volumetric measure (volume_cm3). Useful when comparing product sizes/weights or computing shipping estimates. | Use for: estimate shipping cost proxies using weight and volume; filter products by size/weight thresholds for packaging analysis; join product size to order_items to analyze shipping cost by product dimensions

views.name: leads_closed_enriched
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  lc.mql_id,
  lc.seller_id,
  lc.sdr_id,
  lc.sr_id,
  lc.won_date,
  lc.business_segment,
  lc.lead_type,
  lc.lead_behaviour_profile,
  lc.has_company,
  lc.has_gtin,
  lc.average_stock,
  lc.business_type,
  lc.declared_product_catalog_size,
  lc.declared_monthly_revenue,
  lq.first_contact_date,
  lq.landing_page_id,
  lq.origin
FROM leads_closed AS lc
LEFT JOIN leads_qualified AS lq
  ON lc.mql_id = lq.mql_id

params.when_to_use: When you need a one-row-per-mql_id record describing closed (won) leads enriched with qualification attributes — e.g., reporting attributes of a closed lead such as won_date, seller/sdr/sr owners and qualification metadata from the corresponding leads_qualified row. | When joining closed-lead facts to other tables at the mql_id grain (for example, to attribute revenue or order counts back to the closed lead using mql_id as the key). | When filtering or segmenting closed leads by qualification properties that originate in leads_qualified (first_contact_date, landing_page_id, origin) while retaining the closed-lead context (seller_id, lead_type, business_segment).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view when you need all qualified leads (including non-closed/won leads): this view is derived from leads_closed and therefore excludes any mql_id that never entered leads_closed — reusing it would silently drop non-closed cohort members. | Do not use this view when the desired grain is anything other than mql_id (for example, order_id, seller_id, or customer_id): the view has exactly one row per mql_id and will incorrectly duplicate or aggregate rows if joined to lower-level facts without explicit aggregation. | Do not use this view to compute aggregated metrics (counts, sums, rates) across leads without first ensuring deduplication at mql_id: the view already presents one row per mql_id; aggregating it as if it were event-level data may double-count if you join it to other tables at a finer grain. | Do not use this view to infer the qualification status timeline or attributes that may have changed after the join: the LEFT JOIN pulls attributes from leads_qualified by equality on mql_id only — if leads_qualified contains multiple rows per mql_id in the base table (not visible here) or has time-versioned rows, this view may expose only the row surviving the join semantics and hide temporal differences. | Do not use this view when you need guaranteed inner-join semantics (only mql_ids present in both sources): this view uses a LEFT JOIN from leads_closed to leads_qualified, so it will include closed leads even when there is no matching leads_qualified row; reusing it for analyses that expect only intersected rows will be incorrect.
params.comparison: use leads_qualified (base table) instead when you need the complete set of qualified leads (all mql_id regardless of closed/won status) — leads_closed_enriched has the same qualification columns but is restricted to closed leads (subset) and thus changes cohort size. | use customer_order_agg (AGG) instead when your target analysis is aggregate order-level metrics per customer/seller — customer_order_agg is aggregated at a different grain (customer/seller) appropriate for order summaries whereas leads_closed_enriched is one-row-per-mql_id and lacks order aggregation. | use order_items_enriched (JOIN) or orders_with_review (JOIN) instead when joining to order or item-level facts — those sibling JOIN views are at order/item grains and preserve lower-level detail, while leads_closed_enriched is at the mql_id lead grain and will cause mismatched cardinality if naively joined to order-level tables. | use orders_latest_status_rank (RANK) instead when you need latest-status deduplication or rank-based selection at the order grain — leads_closed_enriched does not perform ranking/deduplication logic and is unsuitable for selecting latest rows in other domains. | use seller_location_lookup (JOIN) when you need seller geographic attributes — that sibling supplies location enrichment keyed by seller, which is more appropriate than reusing this view to attach seller attributes indirectly (leads_closed_enriched contains seller_id but not location fields).

views.description: One row per closed lead (leads_closed) enriched with corresponding qualified-lead attributes when available (leads_qualified). Useful for acquisition funnel analysis linking first contact/lead source to closed deals. | Use for: analyze conversion time from first contact to won_date by origin or landing_page_id; segment won leads by business_segment or declared_monthly_revenue; join closed leads to seller performance metrics
